entries.title: Gemini API's Tool Retrieval loads only the tools a call needs

sources.headline: Tool Retrieval in preview, so agents with big tool libraries only load the details they need

prose: In preview, the Gemini API can search a large tool library and load only the tool details relevant to the current request instead of the whole set — the same token problem as stuffing every MCP tool definition into context on every turn. Worth testing against existing on-demand skill and MCP loading setups.

entries.title: Tabentic puts an agent inside your browser tabs

sources.headline: Put an AI Agent in Your Browser Tabs

prose: A Chrome extension where the agent works in the tabs you already have open: extracting page content into structured formats, summarizing, filling forms, and running repetitive chores across tabs, with an approve-before-execute step. Free tier plus paid plans.

entries.title: Gemini takes over Mac apps and files, asking before it acts

sources.headline: computer use, letting it handle multi-step tasks across your files, desktop apps, and the web in a background window
Google gives Gemini control of your Mac and tightens Android installs

prose: The Gemini app for macOS can now run multistep tasks across files, desktop apps and the web in a background window, and waits for approval before acting — US-only for now, on paid AI plans. The same issue flags Android developer verification going global in January 2027, eventually covering apps installed from anywhere rather than just the Play Store, with new APIs to automate registration in CI.

links.label: Google: Gemini computer use on Mac

entries.title: A swapped model endpoint makes the case for model attestation

sources.headline: Hijacked model answered Prime Intellect customers for two days

prose: Prime Intellect's DeepSeek V4.1 Flash endpoint was replaced with a copy that refused just 1 in 100 jailbreak prompts, and it served customers that way from November 8 to 10. Developers found out through OpenRouter rather than the provider, and the ask afterwards is model attestation: a way to verify that the endpoint you are calling actually runs the model you signed up for. That matters for anything routed through resellers, routers or aggregators.

entries.title: Two weeks of OpenCode plus Qwen on a Mac Studio: what broke

sources.headline: A developer tried to replace Claude Code with a local setup. Here’s what broke

prose: David Gewirtz tried to replace Claude Code with OpenCode plus Qwen's coding model on a 128GB Mac Studio, entirely local — but the harness gave him 64,000 tokens of context against Claude Code's million. A PDF organizer worked on one file and failed on a folder; a 7,000-screenshot renamer ate four days of failed fixes until the context collapsed. His rules worth copying: scrap and restart rather than piling patches on a failing loop, give each feature or bug its own conversation, have the agent write what it learned to a markdown file for the next session, pick the model explicitly, and keep shell commands behind manual approval. Ollama has a one-command setup for the same stack.

entries.title: OpenAI puts full-duplex voice in the API at $0.05 a minute

sources.headline: OpenAI hands devs the voice behind ChatGPT

prose: GPT-Live-1.1 is the same full-duplex voice model ChatGPT Plus and Pro users have had since October 15, now callable from the API. It listens while it speaks and is better at tricky details like letters and numbers, and a standby mode kicks in after 5–60 seconds of silence so idle minutes are not billed at full rate. Active sessions cost $0.05 per minute, which is cheap enough to put a voice front end on an existing agent.

entries.title: World Labs opens Atlas: text to 3D scenes, priced per frame

sources.headline: World Labs has opened Atlas, its latest world model, to the public

prose: Atlas is now self-serve: text or photos in, 3D scenes and camera-controllable video out, exportable as Gaussian splats and polygon meshes for Blender or a game engine. The API is pay-as-you-go — $0.04 for a first 720p frame, $0.008 per additional frame, $5 to turn views into refined splats — with $10 of free credits and an onboarding prompt written for a coding agent. Caveat: AMD closed its roughly $8.2bn acquisition of World Labs on November 16 and has not said what happens to Atlas.

entries.title: ChatGPT Live Dictation streams speech to text on every plan

sources.headline: OpenAI rolls out Live Dictation for ChatGPT, plus an accounting plugin

prose: ChatGPT's dictation now transcribes as you speak instead of waiting until you stop, so the text appears in real time while you talk. It is live on all plans across iOS, Android, web and desktop, which makes it a usable dictation layer anywhere ChatGPT runs. The same rollout adds ChatGPT for Accounting, a plugin that connects to common accounting tools for invoicing and month-end reporting.

entries.title: Kai reviews GitHub pull requests against a semantic map of the codebase

sources.headline: **Catch Bugs With AI Code Reviews**

prose: Instead of reading only the diff, it builds a map of dependencies and connected functions, then posts findings as inline PR comments, with MCP hooks for agents. Useful if you want automated review wired into Hermes repos, though it is hosted — keep private code out or check the deployment options first.

entries.title: ReelRebel finds and cuts short clips from long videos on your own machine

sources.headline: **Turn Long Videos Into Viral Clips**

prose: It scans podcasts and interviews for strong moments, cuts vertical clips, strips dead air and filler words, and adds karaoke captions — processing locally rather than uploading footage. Worth a test on your 4090 box if you ever need to slice up recorded talks or briefings without shipping the files to a cloud editor.

entries.title: Proton Lumo reaches desktop with per-action permission control

sources.headline: Proton brings its privacy-focused Lumo assistant to Windows, Mac, and Linux

prose: Proton's privacy-focused Lumo assistant now ships as desktop apps for Windows, Mac and Linux, and lets you decide which actions the AI may take on its own. Useful as the conservative-by-default option when you want a cloud assistant without handing over blanket agency.

entries.title: Microsoft MAI Code 2 claims 98% of Sol's coding at 40% cost

sources.headline: Microsoft unveils seven new MAI models at Ignite, including MAI Code 2

prose: At Ignite 2026 Microsoft announced seven new MAI models, with MAI Code 2 the one to watch: Microsoft says it delivers 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol's coding performance at 40% of the cost. That makes it a plausible second provider for agent loops where near-Sol code quality at half the bill is good enough.

entries.title: ChatGPT Wallet lets agents pay with a token, not your card

sources.headline: OpenAI Lets AI Agents Shop With Your Money
OpenAI launches a secure way to pay with agents

prose: Built with American Express, Mastercard and Visa, ChatGPT Wallet swaps the card details for a per-purchase payment token, so the agent never sees the number. It is rolling out now, starting on Dots for US ChatGPT Pro subscribers. OpenAI also published commerce guidance for merchants on making a business agent-friendly — the practical piece if you ever want an agent to complete a checkout rather than hand you a link.

entries.title: Anthropic's guide to verifying agent work at scale

sources.headline: Self Verification
How to verify coding agent work at scale

prose: The Claude Code team writes and reviews roughly 90% of its code with Claude, and this write-up explains the verification system behind that. It covers which tests are actually worth investing in, how to build fast verification loops an agent can trust, and how to turn misses into standing rules so you can delegate more without reading every diff.

entries.title: GPT-6.2 Astra cuts to $8/$40, Sol as the lean alternative

sources.headline: 2. OpenAI launches two new models, plus a sales plugin
OpenAI’s cheaper coding models divide devs

prose: OpenAI shipped GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol in Codex and the API, both aimed at finishing the job with fewer output tokens. Astra also takes a 20% price cut to $8/$40 per million input/output tokens, with Sol the cheaper everyday option. Early reviews split: some devs report cleaner code and better reviews, while a CTO says Astra stalls on long tasks and asks baffling questions — the prompting guide is the fast way to judge it against your own harness.

entries.title: A prompt that vets a new library with a graded draft-PR proof

sources.headline: How to find out if your new tech stack is any good

prose: Instead of reading docs to guess whether a library fits, paste this prompt into the agent inside the repo where you would actually use it: research the technology, find the gnarliest existing problem it could address, and build a proof of concept in a draft PR. The agent then grades the attempt on API nuance, typesafety, testability, complexity, docs and deployment changes; a skip verdict means delete the branch. Demoed on the XState v6 beta.

entries.title: Hermes software-factory tutorial: GitHub issues to merged PRs

sources.headline: How to turn Hermes into an autonomous software factory

prose: A walkthrough of running Hermes as an autonomous factory: it watches GitHub issues, writes specs, builds and validates fixes, and opens pull requests with minimal intervention. The video covers installing the factory skill, connecting GitHub, running the first issue end to end, and scheduling the workflow so it keeps working across repos.

entries.title: SID-2 swarms agents for search at $0.25-2 per million tokens

sources.headline: A new Silicon Valley startup beats Opus and Astra at search

prose: San Francisco startup SID attacks web search with teams of up to dozens of cooperating agents instead of one large model. It claims SID-2 beats frontier models like Opus and Astra on search quality while running 8x faster and cutting search cost 20x, priced at $0.25 to $2 per million tokens. The models are callable from sid.ai/models, so it is a candidate replacement for a RAG or search step in your own pipeline.

entries.title: Claude Cowork points a scheduled agent at one folder on your desktop
prose: Anthropic's desktop app now has a Cowork tab that scopes an agent to a single directory, proposes a plan before moving files, and can run prompts on a daily schedule. Worth testing as a low-risk yardstick for Hermes' file and calendar jobs, though it hands Anthropic exactly the data your 4090s keep local.

links.label: Build a research agent, no code

entries.title: A stolen Fireworks AI key seeded a backdoored Claude Code extension in Cursor
prose: Attackers used a stolen Fireworks AI key to publish a trojaned Claude Code extension to Cursor's marketplace, live roughly 11 hours and possibly reaching 5,000 users. Concretely: scope API keys per tool, and review or pin anything your agent stack installs from a marketplace.

entries.title: Omnigraph is an open-source graph database built for agent memory

sources.headline: The week in products

prose: Omnigraph stores agent state as a graph instead of flat vectors, and it self-hosts. That is the piece Hermes lacks when a task needs multi-hop recall across earlier runs, and it runs fine on your own box with no vendor endpoint in the loop.

entries.title: Nod by n8n: open-source personal agent with its own computer

sources.headline: Nod by n8n — Open source personal agent with its own computer

prose: The n8n team's open-source take on a personal agent: instead of bolting tools onto a chat window, the agent gets its own computer to work in. It finished at 306 upvotes on Product Hunt, and it is worth a read for the architecture even if you keep running your own harness.

entries.title: Scribe v3: ElevenLabs speech-to-text, 27% fewer errors in 90+ languages

sources.headline: Scribe v3 by ElevenLabs — Speech to text with 27% fewer errors in 90+ languages

prose: ElevenLabs' third-generation Scribe transcription model claims 27% fewer errors across 90+ languages, making it a drop-in candidate for dictation and meeting-transcript pipelines. It launched to 181 upvotes on Product Hunt and sits alongside the company's TTS and realtime voice stack.

entries.title: Malicious Claude Code update hit ~5,000 Cursor users via SSH backdoor

sources.headline: A stolen Fireworks AI key let attackers plant a backdoored Claude Code extension in Cursor's marketplace
Cursor links hijacked Claude Code extension to Fireworks AI breach

prose: An access key exposed in the Fireworks AI breach let an attacker push a malicious update to the Anthropic Claude Code extension on Cursor's marketplace. Versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 stayed live roughly 11 hours on October 29 and tried to install a persistent SSH backdoor on nearly 5,000 machines. Anyone who installed either version should check for unauthorised SSH access and rotate credentials — the lesson being that a marketplace extension is a supply-chain surface as live as an npm package.

entries.title: Keep agent instruction files sparse so you can see the model fail

sources.headline: 1.2 Model intuition

prose: Varma deliberately keeps his Codex setup light on custom skills and plugins so failures come from the model rather than his own scaffolding. Worth doing before layering system prompts onto a local model: bare Ollama runs separate model gaps from prompt gaps.

entries.title: Run an agent workflow by hand once before scheduling it to repeat

sources.headline: 1.5 Agentic thinking: design agentic workflows and know when to build an AI agent

prose: Varma does the task in a single Codex thread, spends the time teaching the agent to do it correctly, then converts that thread into a recurring automation that messages him on completion. The same sequence fits Hermes: inspect one real run before letting a cron job burn tokens.

entries.title: Triage a wrong RAG answer as retrieval, context, or generation failure

sources.headline: 1.3 Prompting, context engineering, and RAG

prose: Rather than rewriting the prompt when a copilot answer is wrong, the guide splits failures into retrieval, context and generation, each needing a different fix. On a local RAG stack over the 4090s that ordering tells him whether to touch the index, the chunking, or the model itself.

entries.title: WorkOS Relay keeps OAuth tokens out of the agent runtime

sources.headline: You can’t leak a token you never held

prose: Relay holds the user credential server-side; the agent describes the call it wants and Relay attaches the token on the way out, only to allowlisted hosts. That directly targets the weakest part of Hermes-style automation, where any credential in context ends up in logs, traces and error payloads. Worth testing as a broker in front of whatever Hermes currently authenticates with.

links.label: WorkOS blog: delegated access for AI agents

entries.title: Cloudflare Kitesurf runs a browser engine on Workers for agents

sources.headline: Kitesurf (2.1k ⭐)

prose: Kitesurf is Cloudflare's experimental browser engine running entirely on Workers: it parses HTML and CSS, executes JavaScript, renders screenshots and exposes a Chrome DevTools Protocol endpoint, so Puppeteer and other CDP clients drive it as-is. No Chrome image or browser container to keep warm, which turns page rendering for an agent into a per-request cost instead of an always-on machine. Open source on GitHub, 2.1k stars.

entries.title: Liquid AI's d1.2 decision models answer with confidence at $0.02/M

sources.headline: Liquid AI’s new models top the benchmark charts

prose: Liquid AI shipped d1.2 and d1.2-ultra, omnimodal decision models that take text, images and audio and return a structured answer plus a confidence score instead of prose; ultra takes first place on Artificial Analysis's Decision Index. Input starts at $0.02 per million tokens, and when a value is missing they say "not found" rather than inventing it. That makes them a cheap front gate: auto-approve high-confidence calls and send the uncertain ones to review or a larger model.

entries.title: Bland AI's Tofu-1 voices whole soundscapes in real time

sources.headline: Bland AI reveals a voice model that generates entire soundscapes

prose: Tofu-1 does not emit a single clean voice: it generates multiple speakers, overlapping voices and background noise in one output. It is full-duplex, so it hears and speaks simultaneously and keeps thinking while talking, and it separates the speaker's voice from surrounding sound. Bland claims 92% of listeners could not tell it was AI; it ships in early January with a research-preview waitlist open now — relevant for phone-agent testing where the tell is usually the dead air and the sterile background.

entries.title: Anthropic's cookbook shows the inbox, timer and outbox pattern for always-on agents

sources.headline: **Trending Cookbook**

prose: A short architecture guide for agents that keep working between sessions: event inboxes, timers, memory, permissions and an outbox. This is the scaffolding Hermes jobs currently lack if you want them to wake on schedule, remember what happened, and resume after a restart instead of starting cold.

entries.title: Microsoft's TokenEconomizer plugin cuts coding-agent cost by learning each repo

sources.headline: **Top Tool**

prose: A Microsoft plugin that records repo-specific quirks from past sessions, drops tools the agent never calls, and nudges it out of repeated failure loops. The team reports 18.4–30.9% lower mean cost on SWE-Bench across five agent-model combos. It works with Claude Code, Codex and Copilot CLI, so you can trial it on a side repo before wiring it near Hermes.

entries.title: Qwen4-Max: 1M context at $1.50/$4.50, cached input 70% off

sources.headline: Alibaba’s new flagship model won’t break your bank

prose: Alibaba's Qwen4-Max takes a 1M-token context at $1.50/$4.50 per million input/output tokens, with cached input 70% cheaper. The company says it narrowly beats Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol on DeepSWE, though it falls well behind Kimi K3.1 on Terminal-Bench and scores 43 on the Artificial Analysis index — so strong on that one coding benchmark, not necessarily across every task. Available now through Qwen Cloud in the Singapore region.

entries.title: Token Economizer learns your repo to cut agent cost 18–31%

sources.headline: Make your coding agents cheaper the more you use them

prose: Microsoft's open-source plugin (6.8k stars) learns repo-specific quirks from past sessions, prunes tools the agent never touches, and nudges it out of repeated failure loops. On SWE-Bench the team reports 18.4–30.9% lower mean cost across five agent-model combinations. It works with Claude Code, Codex, Copilot CLI and Pi, with experimental support for several others — a drop-in for an existing harness rather than a new one.

entries.title: AppBrain timelines reveal when an app was renamed or pulled

sources.headline: Check other stores and the app's history

prose: AppBrain keeps a dated timeline of an app's publishing history, including unpublishing and later updates under a new name. Useful when a privacy-sensitive app rebrands after bad coverage and you want the old developer trail.

entries.title: Apple's reviews RSS feed returns up to 500 app reviews per country

sources.headline: Analyze the reviews

prose: The iTunes customer-reviews endpoint accepts a country code and app ID and returns JSON, capped at 10 pages of 50 reviews. You can point Hermes at it to batch-collect reviews for an LLM pass instead of scraping the store page.

entries.title: Swapping the App Store country code to IE exposes EU trader details

sources.headline: Gather app store information

prose: Apple's EU listings show a verified trader's DUNS number, address, phone and email when you replace the country segment with 'ie'. Use it to check who actually owns an app and whether the privacy policy matches the registered entity.

entries.title: Exodus Privacy scans Android app IDs for trackers and permissions

sources.headline: Look at what the app does

prose: Exodus Privacy runs a free scan on an Android app ID and reports embedded trackers and requested permissions. That gives you a quick privacy check before installing a vendor APK or recommending a tool, without needing to decompile it yourself.

entries.title: ChromePing places real phone calls from the browser with live two-way translation
prose: A browser app dials any ordinary phone number and translates speech in both directions with running captions; the person answering just picks up their normal phone. Worth a look as a latency reference for live speech translation, though the translation runs in their cloud, not your 4090s.

entries.title: Product Hunt ships an MCP server that puts its launch data inside your assistant
prose: An official MCP server exposes Product Hunt launches, vote counts and topics as tools an assistant can call directly. For Hermes it is a single connector to wire in, letting the agent pull launch data on demand instead of you scraping pages by hand.

entries.title: Subscriptrack finds forgotten subscriptions from email, no bank login

sources.headline: A subscription-finder that doesn’t need your bank details

prose: Subscriptrack works out what you're paying for by reading your email instead of asking for bank credentials, flagging trials that quietly converted, unnoticed price rises and apps nobody uses. The email-only approach is both the privacy argument and a pattern he could reuse in his own inbox tooling, where the receipts already live.

entries.title: ChromePing translates a live phone call both ways from the browser

sources.headline: Talk to anyone by phone, in a language you don't speak

prose: ChromePing calls any real phone number from the browser and translates the conversation live in both directions with captions running underneath. The person on the other end just picks up their normal phone and hears their own language a couple of seconds after you stop talking — no app on their side, which is the useful bit for calling Korean businesses or family.

entries.title: Family Intelligence grades speaker IDs from evidence, offline

sources.headline: How Family Intelligence stops a model from guessing who said what

prose: Their household-memory stack runs entirely on home hardware with pyannote-audio for diarisation and faster-whisper for transcription. To get past SPEAKER_00 vs SPEAKER_01, the prompt tells the model to collect context clues across the conversation — direct address followed by a reply, an explicit "I am John" — then grade its own answer against a rubric: CERTAIN, PROBABLE, POSSIBLE, UNKNOWN, each defined by the evidence it requires. That is a reusable pattern for any speaker-attribution or identity-inference task, since it scores evidence rather than self-reported confidence. The full prompt is published.

entries.title: Tiles runs a private AI assistant locally on Mac and Linux

sources.headline: How Tiles runs a private AI assistant locally

prose: Tiles keeps inference on the machine, so chats never touch its servers and cost does not grow with users — and it borrows the GPU of another machine you own when a laptop is too weak. Identities are device-generated on DIDs and UCANs with no central provider, sync is end-to-end encrypted over Iroh, and chat sharing rides AT Protocol instead of a bespoke backend. Version 0.5.0 Alpha 24 is testable now, and it is one of seven projects Mozilla is backing with up to $500,000 over three years with no equity taken — that call for proposals closes Friday, November 20 at 11:59pm Pacific.

links.label: Mozilla human-scale AI call for proposals

entries.title: HermesOS tour walks through one running Hermes agent setup
prose: Tina's HermesOS video walks through her working agent setup, not just demo features: the schedulers, data sources and glue that keep Tacobot and Lifebot running. Worth checking against your own Ollama box, since the boring jobs she describes — mid-conversation reminders, morning briefs, weekly digests — are the ones that survive past week one and can run fully local.

entries.title: FindDepth writes research reports and checks figures against sources

sources.headline: Research With Verifiable Sources

prose: FindDepth is a paid research assistant that splits a broad question into smaller tasks and produces structured reports from primary sources, verifying each figure against the original document before citing it, with tables and charts, in eight languages. The verification-against-source step is the part worth lifting into his own document pipelines rather than paying for the UI.

entries.title: Archilas gives agents one cited, conflict-resolved memory across tools

sources.headline: Give AI Agents a Shared Memory

prose: Archilas is a memory layer for agents that connects to Slack, Notion, GitHub and Linear, stores each team decision with its source and timestamp, and resolves contradictions when a newer decision replaces an older one. Agents query it over MCP, so Claude Code, Cursor and ChatGPT get current, cited context instead of stale notes. Free and paid tiers.

entries.title: Gemini 4 Hydrogen: 2.5x faster coding at $1.50/$7.50 per million

sources.headline: Google ships a leaner Carbon alternative and launches new smart glasses
Google gives devs a faster coding model

prose: Gemini 4 Hydrogen is a lighter model aimed at the everyday coding tasks you hand off to agents: Google says it finishes jobs 2.5x faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash and scores three times higher on Terminal-Bench 4.1, at a flat $1.50/$7.50 per million input/output tokens. A new Orchestrator in Antigravity pairs it with the heavier Carbon model to get near-Carbon results on 24% less quota, so the usable pattern is cheap model for the inner loop and escalate only when a task stalls.

entries.title: Two-step prompt catches mobile bugs with Chrome DevTools MCP

sources.headline: How to catch mobile bugs before your users do

prose: A design engineer published a two-step QA loop for AI-built frontends that look fine on desktop and break on a phone with bad signal. Install the browser MCP server with `claude mcp add chrome-devtools -- npx chrome-devtools-mcp@latest`, then paste a prompt telling the agent to resize the viewport, emulate touch, throttle to 3G, fix whatever breaks and return before/after screenshots as receipts. The same MCP server works in Cursor and Gemini CLI.

entries.title: LiquidCodec: 74M-param speech codec, 361x realtime on one CPU thread

sources.headline: Liquid AI makes on-device voice agents faster

prose: LiquidCodec is a ~74M-parameter model that turns speech into tokens an LLM can work with and back into audio. Liquid AI says it encodes speech 361x faster than real time on a single CPU thread — roughly 13x faster than Kyutai's Mimi — which means lower-latency streaming voice agents that fit on edge devices. It runs through Hugging Face or llama.cpp, so it can be tried locally without a GPU.

entries.title: OpenWorker open-sources its agent harness SDK and builder skill

sources.headline: OpenWorker Agent Harness SDK

prose: DeepLearning.AI released the OpenWorker Agent Harness SDK — the code that wraps an LLM with context, tools, approvals, memory compaction, credential isolation and sandboxing — plus a builder skill that scaffolds an agent from a prompt: `npx @openworkerai/openworker-harness-builder --agent claude --project .`. It is open source and model-agnostic (OpenAI or Anthropic keys), and Andrew Ng's sample prompt for a directory-restricted file-organising agent with per-move approval is a usable template.

entries.title: Planet AI searches a decade of satellite imagery with natural language

sources.headline: **Tools & Tips**

prose: Planet AI is a free browser app that lets you search ten years of Planet satellite imagery with natural-language prompts and compare before/after views. It is a cloud service, so it won't run on your two-4090 Ollama box and sends your queries to Planet; handy for open-source geospatial checks, not private work.

entries.title: Ace gives agents your real Mac over Tailscale instead of a sandbox

sources.headline: GitHub Next's open-source tool lets teams and agents collaborate on the same Mac

prose: Ace is GitHub Next's open-source tool for agents working on a real machine rather than a hosted sandbox: shared channels where teammates can steer each other's agents, plus direct access to the local shell, tools and apps over Tailscale. For a Mac-based workflow that is the difference between an agent that can drive real apps and one that only sees a container — the same direction as Terminal Mac and agent-desktop, with the human collaboration layer built in.

entries.title: AWS Emulator stubs 200+ services locally so agents can test offline

sources.headline: AWS gives coding agents their own local cloud

prose: AWS shipped an open-source local stand-in for more than 200 of its services so coding agents can run their test loops offline instead of checking every change against the real cloud. That removes the per-call cost and the latency that makes agents stall between iterations, and the emulator itself was written by autonomous agents. AWS's own docs flag the limit: it cannot yet simulate throttling, outages or regional differences, so treat it as a dev-loop accelerator rather than a staging replacement.

entries.title: Gemini Decision 1 scores 1,000 questions in one pass at $0.10/M

sources.headline: Google’s decision model scores 1,000 questions at once

prose: Gemini Decision 1 is a multimodal model built for closed-set decisions: feed it text, images, audio, video or PDFs and it scores up to 1,000 questions in a single pass without generating any output tokens, so your code branches on the probabilities it returns. Typical responses take 150–250ms and it costs $0.10 per million input tokens with no output charges. That makes it the fifth vendor in the decision-model slot this log already tracks — Jev, Microsoft's Decision-1, OpenAI's Decisions API and SubQ Snap — and the first that takes video and PDF inputs.

entries.title: One prompt turns scattered flags into explicit state machines

sources.headline: How to find hidden bugs with one state-machine prompt
How to untangle the state logic in a messy project

prose: A paste-ready prompt for Claude Code or Codex: find every implicit state machine in the app — scattered booleans, flags and status strings — and refactor them into explicit states without breaking anything, trading off user, developer and agent experience. The workflow is commit a checkpoint, paste the prompt, review the diff, then run tests, since "without breaking anything" is an instruction and not a guarantee.

entries.title: United and Amazon now block third-party AI agents from booking and buying

sources.headline: Today’s top stories

prose: United Airlines will bar personal AI agents from booking and checking in, and Amazon already blocks agents from transacting on its site, both citing privacy and fraud risk rather than technical limits. Any Hermes automation pointed at consumer-facing sites should plan for bot detection and account bans, and keep agent work on data and endpoints you already control.

entries.title: Granola ships free voice typing, straight at Wispr Flow

sources.headline: Your favorite notetaker now does the typing too
Granola takes on Wispr with a new dictation tool

prose: Granola, the meeting-notes app, has launched a free voice-typing tool aimed squarely at Wispr Flow's turf. Worth a side-by-side against the paid dictation setup already in use on the Mac: same job — hold a key, talk, get clean text into any app — with no subscription attached, so the question is whether accuracy and latency hold up.

entries.title: Gemini 4 Carbon tops the index at Argon's $2/$10 price

sources.headline: Google makes its strongest model generally available
Gemini Leads the Pack Again
Did Google Just Take the Lead Again?
Google’s new frontier model hunts bugs across codebases
Google announces Gemini 4 Carbon with leading results

prose: Google's second Gemini 4 release in a month ranks #1 on Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index, ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, and is built for long-running engineering work — Google claims it spent days at a time tracking and patching bugs across codebases. It more than doubles Argon's secure-code success rate, cut successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 to zero and blocked every attack in Gray Swan's prompt-injection benchmark. It launches at Argon's introductory $2/$10 per million input/output tokens, with access going first to cyber defenders through Google's Fairwind programme.

entries.title: Boxes.dev gives each agent thread its own cloud computer

sources.headline: Give every Claude Code or Codex thread its own cloud computer

prose: Boxes.dev hands each Claude Code or Codex thread a separate cloud machine, so agents keep running after you close the laptop. You start and steer them from Slack, Linear, phone, desktop or terminal, run several in parallel without worktree collisions, and keep using your existing subscription. Same shape as Cua, boat and Terminal Mac, aimed at the thread rather than the agent.

entries.title: One audit prompt to re-check shipped code on every model release

sources.headline: How to audit your codebase every time a new model ships

prose: An Anthropic engineer runs a single prompt over the project root each time a new model drops: read the whole project, fix everything clearly broken or dead, and list the rest for review. Saved to .claude/commands/audit.md it becomes a /audit slash command you re-run on every release. The value is the habit — newer models find bugs the old ones missed, and shipped code almost never gets re-read.

entries.title: MiniMax-H3-Image ships open weights for native 16MP images

sources.headline: MiniMax gives devs open weights for 16MP images

prose: MiniMax released H3-Image with downloadable weights on Hugging Face, native 4K output in about 10 seconds, editing, and up to 16 reference images. It runs in ComfyUI locally or through the API, accepts 16MP+ jobs, and is half price this week. Anything that heavy belongs on a rented GPU, but the weights mean you can test it without a vendor account.

entries.title: Documented's open TikTok pipeline clusters reuploads with Whisper and embeddings
prose: Documented published its Decoding Immigrant TikTok pipeline on GitHub: a scraper, Whisper transcription, machine translation and a clustering step that groups videos by semantic and containment similarity to flag reuploads. Every component is free and runs on your own device. You could lift the Whisper-plus-clustering half onto the 4090 box to dedupe any local media corpus without sending audio to a cloud API.

entries.title: Exa Monitors runs scheduled web searches that call your agent

sources.headline: Exa Monitors v2 — Web search on a schedule that calls your agent

prose: Exa Monitors v2 runs a saved web query on a schedule and, instead of just mailing a digest, calls your agent with what changed — about $2 per 1,000 runs. That replaces the hand-rolled cron-plus-scraper pattern behind most 'watch this topic' automations, and is relevant to the briefing pipeline, where a monitor could take over part of the fetch loop.

entries.title: Glasshand hands an agent a real iPhone and Mac

sources.headline: Glasshand — Give your agent a real iPhone and Mac

prose: Glasshand puts a real iPhone and Mac on the other end of the agent's loop rather than a simulator, aimed at mobile work emulators cannot reproduce — signing flows, push, carrier or hardware-dependent behaviour. It shipped on Product Hunt with about 400 upvotes. Same category as TapKit: worth a look if iOS testing is ever the blocker.

entries.title: One AGENTS.md paragraph stops agents bolting features onto bad architecture

sources.headline: How to stop AI agents from bolting on features

prose: A one-paragraph addition at the top of AGENTS.md (Cursor, Codex) or CLAUDE.md (Claude Code) tells the agent to build modularly with proper separation of concerns and, if there is no natural place for the feature, to stop before writing code and propose the refactor instead. The last sentence does the work — it converts a silent architectural compromise into a question you can answer.

entries.title: 0 Security turns a coding agent into an open-source security harness

sources.headline: Turn your coding agent into an open-source security harness

prose: 0 Security (1.2k stars) packages code review, vulnerability investigation, app pentesting, binary reverse engineering, finding verification and the fix loop behind one web UI. CLI and MCP support mean the same workflows can be plugged straight into an existing agent, so it is a wrapper to point at your own repos rather than another dashboard to babysit.

entries.title: Warp's open-source /merge-risk skill scores a PR before you read it

sources.headline: 5 questions to decide how much human review a PR needs

prose: Warp's agent-factory lead published a five-check triage for the review queue — verification (screenshots or recordings of before/after, required on every PR), alignment against the original issue, impact (auth, permissions and billing need an owner; split high-impact work into stacked PRs), rollback cost (two-way versus one-way doors, per Matt Pocock's framing) and error detection (Sentry alerts piped to agents by webhook so they can investigate their own bugs). The five checks ship as an open-source /merge-risk skill the agent runs before handing over a PR, and the cheapest start is two extra PR-template fields: impact and rollback cost.

entries.title: Meta's Muse Ember: $0.10/M input tokens for high-volume agent calls

sources.headline: Meta’s smallest model is built for repeating agentic work

prose: Muse Ember is Meta's smallest, cheapest model at $0.10 per million input tokens — level with Claude Haiku and GPT-6 Luna, and competitive with open-weight options like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. It is aimed squarely at high-volume agent work: tool calls, routing, data extraction and smaller coding jobs, with Meta recommending you pair it with Muse Wonder as the planner that handles the thinking while Ember handles the volume.

entries.title: Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small: open weights with strong vision

sources.headline: Thinking Machines debuts its second-generation AI model

prose: Thinking Machines' second-generation model targets long-running coding, research and office work, with vision as the standout skill — it picked three wines from a single photo 19 times out of 20, beating the lab's own researchers in a blind test. It is live now on Tinker, where it can be called like any API, and is expected to land at the top of DesignArena's open-weight leaderboard with full weights promised next week.

entries.title: OpenCode Browse hands agents your real logged-in browser

sources.headline: Let coding agents use your real browser, with your existing tabs, logins, and extensions

prose: OpenCode Browse lets a coding agent drive your actual browser instead of a headless sandbox with no session, so existing tabs, logins and extensions all work. It plugs into OpenCode, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and other MCP clients, opens its tabs quietly in the background, and hands control back to you for logins, 2FA or payments before continuing.

entries.title: Claude Code's allowlist leaked 1,379 secrets to public GitHub

sources.headline: Anthropic’s coding agent is leaking your secrets to GitHub

prose: Claude Code stores its approved-command allowlist in plain text, so every "don't ask again" entry that carried a password or API key sits on disk in the clear. Apiiro found 1,379 secrets across 1,122 copies of that settings file in public GitHub repositories; users flagged it in 2025 and the reports went unfixed until Claude Code lead Boris Cherny said the team is finally looking at a fix. Immediate action: rotate any key that ever passed through an approval prompt, add the settings file to .gitignore, and pass secrets as environment variables instead of inline.

entries.title: Maigret sweeps a username across thousands of sites and repairs broken checkers

sources.headline: Tools tested

prose: Maigret is the long-running open-source CLI checker, with site definitions that a built-in mechanism tests and self-repairs when they stop working. Useful as a periodic self-audit of your own handles; full scans are noisy, at 70 percent plus false positives in this testing, so pair it with a validating tool like Helix.

entries.title: Consensus-OSINT bundles 19 OSINT datasets behind one scan and an MCP server

sources.headline: AI features

prose: Consensus-OSINT aggregates Maigret, WhatsMyName, Sherlock and sixteen other projects, and ships an MCP server so an assistant can call it directly. That is the shape Hermes wants for any recon or exposure check: one tool endpoint instead of five CLIs. About 1,200 of 8,161 checks came back blocked in testing, so treat nulls as unknown, not absent.

entries.title: Helix re-checks every username hit with fake control probes to cut false positives

sources.headline: Additional validation

prose: Helix is an open-source CLI username search covering roughly 11,000 sites that re-queries each hit with three made-up usernames and drops any site that "finds" those too. Running it on your own handles from the 4090 box shows what is publicly reachable without handing the query to a web service. Blocked and timed-out sites are listed as not-checked rather than not-found.

entries.title: PasteGuard strips secrets from the clipboard before chat sees them

sources.headline: A copy-paste app that makes privacy easier

prose: PasteGuard checks the clipboard locally and swaps sensitive values — database URLs, credentials, keys — for placeholders before they land in an AI chat, so the copy-paste habit stays exactly the same. The maker built it after pasting a production config into a chat himself. Pairs with the egress-masking tools already in the log: this one sits at the paste, before anything leaves the machine.

entries.title: Friday Work hands a stalled task to another agent mid-run

sources.headline: Friday Work ↗ — When Claude hits its limit, your task keeps going

prose: Friday is a task board that runs Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and a dozen other agents side by side on his own machine, letting them message each other. When one hits its usage limit the task moves to another agent carrying a record of what it already changed, so a Claude limit at four in the afternoon stops being the end of the day. The failover-with-change-log part is the piece the parallel-agent setups in the log are missing.

entries.title: MachineMail gives each agent its own inbox and verification flow

sources.headline: MachineMail ↗ — Real inboxes for AI agents, with trust built in

prose: MachineMail hands an agent a real email address so it can sign itself up for a service, sit and wait for the verification code, and answer whatever comes back. Inboxes are created on demand, a catch-all domain covers the rest, and wait_for_message is the call that blocks until mail arrives. Trust and provenance controls are part of the design rather than bolted on — the missing piece for agents that need an account, not a human in the loop.

entries.title: Beacon — open-source self-improving memory for coding agents

sources.headline: beacon.sh — Open-source self-improving memory for AI coding agents
Open-source self-improving memory for AI coding agents

prose: Beacon is an open-source memory layer for coding agents that rewrites itself as it learns, from asymptote-labs. It targets the same gap as a hand-maintained AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, but updates the stored context from the agent's own runs instead of waiting for him to prune it. Worth a read for the retrieval and update design even if he keeps his file-based setup.

entries.title: Filter the data with regexes before the model reads it

sources.headline: How to run an agent over millions of rows without blowing your budget

prose: Karpathy built a YouTube feed out of 43 million Hacker News comments without feeding them to a model: he filtered first with URL matching, regexes, dedupe and spam removal, then had Sonnet read only the survivors — 6,454 recommended videos in about two hours. The reusable prompt asks the agent to write a filter script that prints row counts before and after and calls no model; tighten it until the residue is small, then switch to the cheap model to read it. Same recipe for any giant log or export.

links.label: The Code — Karpathy's better YouTube feed

entries.title: Cheap executor subagent cuts cost per PR from $80 to $20

sources.headline: How to cut your cost per PR without losing quality

prose: Warp's founder took cost per PR from $80 to $20 with fewer reverts by splitting planning from execution: set the main session to a strong model (Opus 5.5 via /model) to plan, then add .claude/agents/executor.md with "model: haiku" and tools pinned to Read, Edit and Grep, instructed never to change the plan or touch files outside it. Ask for a plan, tell Claude to use the executor subagent for each step, and compare cost per PR before and after. The subagent-file version of the advisor trick already in the log.

entries.title: OpenAI's Decisions API returns a choice or score, not prose

sources.headline: Your App Doesn’t Need an Essay. It Needs a Decision.

prose: Give Decisions API context (text, images or JSON), a question and the allowed answers or a scoring rubric, and it returns a focused choice, probability or score instead of a paragraph. Fits the cheap decision-model pattern already in the log: routing billing vs. support vs. account requests, scoring damage from a photo, grading severity on ordered levels, or letting an agent pick continue / retry / ask-for-clarification mid-run.

entries.title: Siri App Intents open to developers in the iOS 27.3 beta

sources.headline: Apple Opens Siri AI to Third-Party Apps
Developers can finally get Siri to take actions in apps

prose: Apple rolled out a Developer Preview in the iOS 27.3 betas that lets apps plug into Siri AI through App Intents: you declare which data and actions Siri may touch, chain them into workflows, and drive multi-step tasks like checkout with markdown-based skills. Testing is limited to internal TestFlight builds for now, with users getting access in a few months and App Store submissions in spring — so this is the window to build against the real API rather than a demo.

entries.title: Burn expiring Codex quota with a /goal cleanup run

sources.headline: How to burn leftover Codex quota before it resets

prose: For quota that resets half-unused: turn on the goals feature with `goals = true` under `[features]` in the Codex config, then give it a cleanup goal like `/goal Remove all dead code nothing calls, verified by passing tests` — it keeps working across turns until the goal is met. The thread adds four more targets: duplicated logic, unused dependencies, stale sessions and zombie scheduled tasks.

links.label: The Code — the four extra targets

entries.title: Cutting CI wait from 40 minutes to 2 so agents stop stalling

sources.headline: How to make your CI 20x faster

prose: Boardy's head of engineering breaks down how his team took PR wait times from 40 minutes to 2: where the pipeline actually loses time, what is worth caching or running in parallel, and how to run smarter tests so coding agents never sit blocked on a build. The agent-specific point is the loop time — a slow CI turns every agent iteration into a coffee break.

entries.title: Untangle Codebase skill strips cruft so agents can navigate the repo

sources.headline: Untangle Codebase

prose: An agent skill you point at a repo from Claude Code, Cursor or Codex: it removes copy-paste, leaky abstractions, temporary workarounds and pointless wrappers so the code is easier for both you and the agent to read and change. Aimed at the accumulated cruft of months of vibe coding, before the codebase becomes unmaintainable.

entries.title: Open-source local Wispr Flow clone for Mac dictation

sources.headline: A dev reverse-engineered the paid dictation app Wispr Flow

prose: A developer reverse-engineered Wispr Flow — the paid, cloud dictation app — and published an open-source version that runs entirely on the Mac, with benchmarks the issue calls super-impressive (2.5K bookmarks on the thread). Same niche as Hex: hold a key, talk, and the text lands in whatever app has focus, which is the fastest way to dictate long prompts into a coding agent instead of typing them. Running locally means no audio leaves the machine.

entries.title: VISTA keeps every frame an agent sees and lets it zoom back

sources.headline: Context Engineering for Images

prose: MIT's VISTA drops the usual embed-and-delete pattern: it stores every frame a vision-language agent receives, plus the actions and their results, and gives the agent a tool to retrieve and zoom into any of them, with separate notes for environment-level and level-specific facts. On ARC-AGI-3 it hit a perfect 100 RHAE with Claude Opus 5.0 (fewer actions than first-time humans; 99 with GPT-5.6 Sol), and 63.3% of GameWorld tasks against 40% for the native harness — the ablation without frame storage fell to 70 RHAE. The harness is open under the MIT licence; it is the image analogue of text context engineering.

entries.title: Indicator workshop shows free alerts for new mentions and page changes

sources.headline: **This week on Indicator**

prose: Craig posted the video, transcript, and AI-generated notes from the October workshop on setting up free alerts that catch new mentions of people, companies, and phrases, plus tracking changes to webpages. Those watch loops map directly onto Hermes triggers without adding another paid monitoring subscription.

entries.title: Pangram's image detector flags AI edits, but cropping still evades it

sources.headline: **Deception in the News**

prose: Pangram, known for its text detector, released an image detector it says scored 99.96% on 1,200 synthetic images; aggressive cropping still fools it. Useful if he wants to check an image before trusting it, and a reminder the verdict cannot separate lightly edited from fully generated.

entries.title: Spotlight 2.0 runs a swarm of OSINT agents on your own machine

sources.headline: **This week on Indicator**

prose: The Indicator Lab shipped Spotlight 2.0, an agentic investigation system that coordinates a swarm of AI agents for OSINT research and can run locally on your own hardware. A multi-agent research loop hosted on the two 4090s is a pattern worth borrowing for Hermes work, and nothing leaves the box.

entries.title: Apple and Goldman start rationing employee AI tokens

sources.headline: 3. Apple and Goldman Sachs restrict employee AI use for different reasons
Apple cuts daily AI spending limits for its engineers

prose: Apple reportedly cut some engineers' daily AI spending caps from $300 to $200 last month, with certain teams heading to $100 and anything more needing a senior-leadership exemption. Goldman Sachs limited AI coding tools to engineering, cutting off most traders and bankers over security — a reversal from its CIO praising vibe coding in July — and Meta and Microsoft made similar moves in October.
